deep.reconstruction:
This page is part of §5–6 of Riemann's Habilitationsschrift 'Über die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe' (1854, published by Dedekind in 1867). The folio is a fair copy of the text as published, page 25 of the manuscript.

(A) End of the integrability proof for the example f(x)=Σ (nx)/n² from the previous page, and for any bounded function with the same two properties:
(i) one-sided limits f(x±0) exist everywhere;
(ii) for every σ>0 only finitely many jumps have size ≥σ.
Riemann's criterion (§5) says f is integrable iff, for every σ>0, the total length of subintervals where the oscillation exceeds σ can be made arbitrarily small as the mesh d→0. Given (i) and (ii), choose d so small that:
- on every subinterval not containing one of the finitely many large jumps, the oscillation is <σ (this uses the one-sided limits and compactness; this step is mine);
- the subintervals containing the large jumps, of which there are finitely many, have total length ≤ (number of jumps)·2d, which is arbitrarily small.
So f is integrable.

(B) Remark: a function without infinitely many maxima and minima (piecewise monotone, in modern terms), at points where it stays finite, automatically has properties (i) and (ii). Monotone pieces have one-sided limits, and a bounded monotone function has only finitely many jumps ≥σ. Hence such a function is integrable wherever it is finite. Riemann adds that the example f does not belong to this class: it increases with slope n between jumps but has a dense set of downward jumps. He also says this can easily be shown directly.

(C) Improper integrals at an isolated singularity x=0, where f(x)→+∞ as x↓0.
1. Necessity claim. If x f(x) > C > 0 for all 0<x≤a, then ∫_x^a f(t)dt > C∫_x^a dt/t = C(log(1/x) − log(1/a)) → ∞. So the improper integral diverges. Hence, if x f(x) is not wildly oscillating (no infinitely many maxima and minima near 0), the limit of x f(x) exists. Since it cannot stay above any C>0, convergence of ∫_0 f forces x f(x) → 0.
2. Sufficiency claim. Write f(x)x^α = (1−α) f(x)dx / d(x^{1−α}), using d(x^{1−α}) = (1−α)x^{−α}dx. If x^α f(x) → 0 for some α<1, then |f| ≤ ε x^{−α} near 0. This is integrable, so the integral converges as the lower limit → 0.
3. Start of the logarithmic scale. Note that −d log log(1/x) = dx/(x log(1/x)), so f(x) x log(1/x) = f dx / (−d log log(1/x)). Likewise f x log(1/x) log log(1/x) = f dx / (−d log log log(1/x)). The same argument as in step 1 then shows that, if ∫ f converges, these products cannot stay above a positive constant. The conclusion is completed on the next page: these products must tend to 0 in the non-oscillating case. Conversely, x·log(1/x)⋯log^{n−1}(1/x)·(log^n(1/x))^α f(x) → 0 with α>1 suffices for convergence. This is the Abel/Bertrand–De Morgan logarithmic scale for integrals.
errors: No mathematical errors. The argument tacitly uses f>0 near 0, which is justified because f grows beyond every bound there.

'x f(x) cannot stay above C' only gives liminf x f(x) ≤ 0; turning this into lim x f(x) = 0 needs eventual monotonicity of x f(x). Riemann encodes this in the hypothesis 'no infinitely many maxima and minima', which strictly speaking must refer to x f(x) and not to f.
The step 'choose d so that oscillation <σ on intervals not containing large jumps' needs a compactness argument. Riemann calls it 'offenbar'; it is true but not spelled out.

results.what: A bounded function with one-sided limits everywhere and only finitely many jumps ≥σ (for each σ) is Riemann integrable; applied to Riemann's function Σ(nx)/n², which is discontinuous on a dense set.
results.modern_name: Integrability of regulated functions via Riemann's oscillation criterion

results.what: Piecewise monotone (finitely many extrema) functions are integrable where bounded.
results.modern_name: Integrability of monotone / piecewise monotone functions

results.what: Necessary condition x f(x)→0 and sufficient condition x^α f(x)→0 (α<1) for convergence of the improper integral ∫_0 f; beginning of the logarithmic comparison scale.
results.modern_name: Comparison test for improper integrals; Abel–Bertrand–De Morgan logarithmic scale
results.usually_credited_to: Abel (posthumous), De Morgan and Bertrand (1842), later du Bois-Reymond; Riemann's formulation published 1867
